title: Vercel Blob now supports TTLs for automatic deletion
summary:
Vercel Blob can now delete blobs automatically. Pass ttlDays when you write a blob and it is deleted that many days after upload, from 1 to 730 days. The TTL counts from the blob's upload date.

Use TTLs for blobs you would otherwise delete yourself, such as session transcripts, exports, and temporary uploads.

ttlDays works on put(), copy(), putImage(), multipart uploads, and presigned upload URLs. Every write result and head() response now includes expiresAt, so you know when a blob is due for deletion.

setTtl() changes or removes the TTL of blobs you already have, one URL or up to 1,000 at a time, without re-uploading them.

In Vercel CLI 65.16.0 and later, pass --ttl-days to vercel blob put, put-image, copy or presign, and use vercel blob set-ttl on existing blobs.

Setting a TTL costs one Advanced Operation per started 60 days, on top of the write. A 7-day TTL costs one, and the 730-day maximum costs 13. Clearing a TTL and the deletions themselves are free. You can track TTL operations in the Blob section of the Observability tab.

npm install @vercel/blob@2.9.0

Learn more in the Vercel Blob documentation.

title: Speed Insights now measures soft navigations
summary:
Speed Insights now measures soft navigations: client-side route changes that update page content without a full reload. This means you can now track performance as users move through your app, not just on full-page loads.

Speed Insights captures LCP, FCP, INP, and CLS for soft navigations and includes these measurements in your Real Experience Score. TTFB is not captured because there is no new document request.

Soft-navigation tracking is enabled by default for all projects using Speed Insights, with no action required. It works with modern web frameworks such as Next.js, SvelteKit, and Nuxt, in Chromium-based browsers.

In your project's Speed Insights dashboard, use the new Navigation Type filter to view All, Hard, or Soft navigation data.

Soft-navigation events count toward Speed Insights Plus usage. Existing Plus customers will receive an email with details about when billing for these events begins. For projects that newly enable Plus, these events are billed from the start.

To disable soft-navigation tracking, set softNavs to false in your application code and redeploy. This option requires @vercel/speed-insights version 2.1.0 or later:

Learn more in the Speed Insights documentation.

title: Introducing eve 1.0
summary:
Today we're announcing eve 1.0, the open-source framework for building production-ready agents.

Since the public preview in June, we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available.

We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite.

With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead.

Build production agents on a harness you own

The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in.

For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation.

Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product.

Thousands of businesses already run eve in production for internal and customer-facing agents. Rillet built a software factory on eve that takes in customer requests, converts them into specs, tests the changes, and opens PRs for human review. Rillet tripled its shipping rate in three months. Clay built monty, a data agent that answers employees’ questions in Slack. Just over two months in, 30–40% of the company used it every week.

Lindy's agent framework roundup names eve “Best for durable backend agents”.

Collaborate in multiplayer agent sessions

Multiplayer lets several people work with an agent in one shared session. eve keeps track of who said what and directs approvals and sign-ins to the right person. You can set up memory for each user or the whole team.

In the native Slack channel, each thread is one shared session. Approvals appear as buttons that only the right person can answer, and a live task card shows progress and timing. You can follow up in the thread without mentioning the agent again, cancel the current turn, or reset the session from Slack.

Ambient mode lets an agent listen in channels you choose, even without being mentioned. Guided by goals you set per channel, it decides when to speak up, help, or take on a task, and when to stay quiet. To limit model costs, a small decision model screens every message first, and only the ones that might be for the agent start a turn.

Slack is one of several native channels, alongside Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, GitHub, Linear, Twilio, Web Chat, and iMessage. The Chat SDK channel adds support for any Chat SDK platform adapter, including WhatsApp, Messenger, Google Chat, and email. Each channel is one file, and the same agent can work across all of them. See the integrations directory for the full list.

Build agent UIs with Next.js and other frameworks

eve 1.0 expands our native integrations for Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, TanStack Start, and Vite. The framework integrations build your agent alongside your app and set up its routes. On Vercel, you can deploy the agent and your site as one project, or host them separately.

The client libraries let you work with tool calls, approval requests, and questions in a consistent way across frameworks. Use that session data to build custom UIs: stream replies into agent chats, embed an agent in a page, or show the agent's tool calls in your own components.

Use eve add channel/web to scaffold a chat app with AI Elements components, or add eve's React, Vue, or Svelte bindings to an existing UI.

Build multi-tenant agents

One support-agent deployment can connect to each customer's ticketing system with their own credentials and apply that customer's approval rules.

Your application authenticates the user and identifies which tenant they belong to. You can then set memory, connection credentials, and approval policy for that tenant and user.

Before each model call in the main agent loop, dynamic definitions load the agent's capabilities from the session and external data. In 1.0, they cover models, connections, and subagents as well as tools, skills, and instructions.

Give agents memory across sessions

We added native memory so agents can carry context from one session to the next. You choose the memory's scope and can use the built-in file memory, a memory provider, or one you build yourself.

Built-in fileMemory keeps data in memory in eve dev and in a private Vercel Blob store you configure on Vercel.

Other providers include claude-mem, Hindsight, Kybernesis Arcana, Memanto, memco, Supermemory, and Upstash AgentKit.

Trace agents with OpenTelemetry

We rebuilt eve’s tracing around OpenTelemetry, so you can follow an agent’s work in the tracing tools you already use. eve dev records traces locally by default. If you host eve yourself, you can export them to an OpenTelemetry backend, including one you run yourself.

Tracing integrations include Raindrop, with more options in the integrations directory. Add one with eve add instrumentation/, or use the instrumentation APIs to build your own integration.

Traces now show when an agent is waiting for a person, including tool approvals, questions, budget prompts, and sign-ins. They record model selections and approval decisions alongside model usage and cost, and follow calls into MCP servers and remote agents.

You choose what eve collects for tracing. Content you exclude from collection stays out of every destination. You can filter out spans or redact inputs and outputs per destination. Private conversations in production send only metadata by default, without prompts or tool results. The OpenTelemetry guide explains these controls.

On Vercel, Agent Runs uses the same traces to show sessions, model calls, tool execution, subagent activity, and approval decisions in the dashboard. When eve deploy creates a new Vercel project, it sets up trace sampling automatically. See the Agent Runs guide for setup and configuration.

Lower agent turn latency

At the start of September, our hosted stress test on Vercel Workflows took a median of 3.036s per turn. In 1.0, the same 100-turn workload took 414ms. The test sends messages one at a time, with one immediate mock-model response and no tool calls per turn. We measure from sending a message until the turn finishes, capturing eve and Workflow overhead without the time a model takes to generate a response.

We worked with the Workflow team on spec 9, which gives each run a single orchestrator so background steps no longer replay the workflow. The team also moved event and stream writes to WebSockets and cut redundant history reads. eve agents get these improvements through Workflow SDK.

eve also caches the information it needs to route messages to each session and can move idle sessions to a newer deployment between turns. Web UIs can prewarm a session before the first message arrives, so the first reply starts sooner.

Lower workflow costs for long agent sessions

For a 50-turn Evo Docs session, the estimated Vercel Workflows cost drops from 5.4¢ to 1.3¢, about 76% lower. That assumes roughly two model steps per turn and 30-day retention. eve now uses Workflow SDK 5.5 and saves only the conversation data that changed between turns. We've also cut repeated work in workflow steps, checkpoints, and sandbox setup:

  • Workflow steps save changes and refer back to data already stored, instead of repeatedly copying a growing conversation into each step. Steps that don't need history no longer receive it.

  • Checkpoints store references to image files returned by tools, so they don't have to copy the image bytes each time.

  • Sandboxes from prepared snapshots skip repeated setup. Stop a sandbox and keep its files for reuse. Cleanup starts when the session ends.

The storage changes are part of the open-source Workflow SDK, so agents you host yourself on other Workflow backends also store less duplicate session data. The cost estimate above uses Vercel Workflows pricing.

On Vercel, workflow steps run on Fluid compute. They need extra storage writes for inputs above the payload size limit, so sending less session data helps keep turn times consistent as sessions grow. Images and files can still require those writes.

For model calls, tool and skill listings can stay out of the initial prompt until they're needed. Connection tools run through eve__search and eve__tool, so each search no longer has to expand the model's tool list. We also changed how eve marks parts of a prompt for provider caching, so more content can be reused between calls.

Share agent capabilities with extensions

Since the preview, we've added extensions so teams can share tools, skills, instructions, connections, channels, schedules, hooks, and subagents without copying files between agents. You can use extensions from the extensions directory or create your own with npx eve@latest extension init .

For example, agent-browser adds browser automation, Mux Video adds tools for video assets and clips, and Link adds wallet and purchase tools.

eve builds workspace extensions from source and reloads changes during development. You can update shared capabilities in one package and try the changes in your agents as you work.

Build coding agents with eve’s shared tools

The 1.0 code extension builds on eve’s default file tools, adding coding instructions and skills that follow your repository’s AGENTS.md. It's included in the eve package, so there's nothing extra to install. Give it a repository in its sandbox and your agent can investigate code, edit files, and run the project's checks. It uses the same harness and extension system as your other agents, so you can replace or disable tools, override skills, and add your own instructions.

See the benchmark results for comparisons with other coding harnesses using the same tasks and model.

The companion eve/extensions/git adds GitHub and pull request workflows, using credentials and authorization you configure. On Vercel, the optional remote self-modification extension lets your agent propose changes to its own source in a draft pull request. You review the changes, merge them, and deploy.

Build with the same public APIs eve uses

We built eve's subagents, sleep, and question tools on the same workflow system you can use through defineWorkflowTool. Your tools can return a result, start a background task, or keep accepting messages as a resumable task. They can wait for a person, webhook, or timer without keeping compute running, and their runs survive restarts. You don't need a separate background-job system to coordinate that work.

Upgrade to eve 1.0

If you already have an eve agent, the 1.0 upgrade guide walks through the changes to extension builds, agent APIs, session events, clients, and saved history. Follow it before deploying your upgrade.

eve follows semantic versioning, so breaking changes to stable APIs only happen in major releases. Experimental and internal APIs, including experimental fields, can change between major releases.

If your selected team has AI Gateway access, you can start chatting without creating a Vercel project or copying an API key. eve can use your existing Vercel CLI credentials to call models through AI Gateway locally. Use /login to sign in to other connections.

title: Decision-1.1 now available on AI Gateway
summary:
Decision-1.1 from Microsoft AI is now available on AI Gateway. It is more accurate, better calibrated, and faster than Decision-1.

The decision model returns structured answers instead of free-form text for tasks such as routing support requests, choosing which model should handle a request, selecting the next step in a workflow, or grading AI responses.

  • Boolean: the probability that a condition is true

title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
summary:
Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.

Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery, Selection, Access, and Success.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.

That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.

That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one.

The agentic testing pyramid

If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?”

We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid, the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite.

To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success, that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome.

An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, are E2E evals.

Example

Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans.

Here’s a typical request from one of your customers:

Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission.

Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am:

  • Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature)

  • 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget)

  • Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time)

  • Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three)

Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans:

How to build an end-to-end eval

We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor, an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.

Here are the terms we’ll use:

  • Task: one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded

  • Variant: the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills

  • Trial: one attempt by one variant at one task

  • Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each

  • Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output

Step 1: Set a goal

Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier).

Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:

  • Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail

  • Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn

  • Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate

For example, your goal might be to:

  • Increase the success rate on a specific task

  • Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal

  • Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it

  • A/B test a prompt

  • Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why

Example

We looked in all three places for sfbeans:

  • Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.

  • Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.

  • Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.

That gives us our goal:

Goal

Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for

Agents

Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from.

In scope

Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans.

Out of scope

Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later.

Done when

Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time.

Step 2: Define metrics

Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:

Success

  • Success rate: the share of trials that pass

  • Pass@k: the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)

  • Pass^k: the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)

Efficiency (measured on successful trials only)

  • Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

Example

Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway) on the iced latte order could look like:

What the numbers mean:

  • Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.

  • Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.

  • Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.

  • Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.

  • Time: ~3:50 on successful trials.

  • Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s iced-latte-mission:

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Example

Two agents, Claude Code and Codex, with two models each, make four variants.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Step 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Example

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:

Run harbor view jobs to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order. No quote. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Automated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. event_model_payload.headline: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
event_model_payload.summary:
Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.

Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery, Selection, Access, and Success.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.

That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.

That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one.

The agentic testing pyramid

If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?”

We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid, the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite.

To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success, that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome.

An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, are E2E evals.

Example

Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans.

Here’s a typical request from one of your customers:

Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission.

Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am:

  • Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature)

  • 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget)

  • Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time)

  • Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three)

Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans:

How to build an end-to-end eval

We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor, an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.

Here are the terms we’ll use:

  • Task: one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded

  • Variant: the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills

  • Trial: one attempt by one variant at one task

  • Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each

  • Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output

Step 1: Set a goal

Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier).

Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:

  • Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail

  • Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn

  • Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate

For example, your goal might be to:

  • Increase the success rate on a specific task

  • Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal

  • Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it

  • A/B test a prompt

  • Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why

Example

We looked in all three places for sfbeans:

  • Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.

  • Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.

  • Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.

That gives us our goal:

Goal

Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for

Agents

Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from.

In scope

Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans.

Out of scope

Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later.

Done when

Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time.

Step 2: Define metrics

Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:

Success

  • Success rate: the share of trials that pass

  • Pass@k: the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)

  • Pass^k: the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)

Efficiency (measured on successful trials only)

  • Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

Example

Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway) on the iced latte order could look like:

What the numbers mean:

  • Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.

  • Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.

  • Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.

  • Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.

  • Time: ~3:50 on successful trials.

  • Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s iced-latte-mission:

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
summary:
When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits.

Last year, we shipped just that, with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it.

More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged.

  • The first is automation: Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines.

  • The second is agents and harnesses: Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too.

As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance.

Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three.

More secure workflows

The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection.

Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end, before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools.

Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel

On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change:

Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log.

Encryption on self-hosted Worlds

Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams.

A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management. Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay:

More security work in v5

Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads.

You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0, inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability.

A redesigned trace viewer

The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development.

Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets.

Workflows in every region

In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1. Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress.

For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region. Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path.

By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration:

To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start(). That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay:

The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1.

Infrastructure reliability

Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover.

With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors.

As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug.

Agent-ready performance

In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today.

Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit.

In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes.

The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures.

Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers:

Fewer queue hops

In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout.

The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms.

Incremental replay

Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log: replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms. The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes.

WebSocket streaming

Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default. In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds.

Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression.

These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application.

Worlds: the shared durability primitive

Workflow SDK’s durable functions sit on a World: the interface for storing progress, dispatching work, and delivering streams. That same foundation also now supports fx and durable-harness, which adds durability to existing agent harnesses.

Improvements to the shared storage, queue, and streaming infrastructure can benefit any consumer of a World. Optimizations inside the Workflow replay runtime apply to Workflow SDK; they do not automatically apply to every harness.

Choose the integration around how you want to build:

  • Workflow SDK: write durable application logic with use workflow and use step.

  • WorkflowAgent: use @ai-sdk/workflow for an AI SDK agent loop inside a workflow.

  • fx: embed and extend a native coding agent with libfx.

  • durable-harness: keep an existing supported harness and add durability beneath it.

    • Supports Pi and OpenCode, with experimental integrations for Claude Code and Codex in Vercel Sandbox.

  • eve: build agents with durable sessions powered natively by Workflow SDK and Worlds.

We’ll soon be adding more offerings to our catalog of SDKs and frameworks backed by Worlds for durability.

Build with Workflow SDK 5

Besides the improvements above, Workflow SDK 5 also adds:

  • In-flight cancellation with AbortController

  • Searchable run attributes

  • More framework integrations

  • And more
